doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Click tracks, frame counts and calculating chase cues
summary: He explains click-track mathematics, the Carroll Knudson book and cue sheets for chase scenes.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: And you had to learn how to work with a click track in your ear while you’re conducting?

That’s correct. It was, yeah, it was a whole separate science of how to make some hit, some chord or some thing in the music hit at exactly the right time where the gun is fired or the car takes off or there’s some bit of, you know, so there was a whole lot of

mathematics involved. Once you decide what the right tempo is, what feels right, you can then determine what that is in terms of a metronome beat, which of course you have to translate to frames per second, a 12-frame click — well film runs at 24 frames per second. So a 24-frame click meant it went one click every second. A 12-frame click, half of that, would be a click every half a second. And then everything in between. So there was this book the Carroll Knudson book. And this guy should have gotten an award for patience because to mathematically calculate what — every page was a different click number and it was 12-1 in other words 12 and 1 sprocket hole; 12-2 — 12 frame and 2 sprocket holes, based on the film of course. So he calculated every beat from zero to, well as many calculations as a full page, you know, a computer page turned sideways would accommodate all the way to the last thing, which sometimes could go well into 8, 9, 10 minutes. So you know you’ve got to look at this book, where does the thing I want to hit fall? Okay? That’s click number 37. All right well then you’ve got to manipulate your music in order to accommodate that hit. And that’s the kind of thing, that was it. I mean sometimes it took as long — oh those chase scenes especially. Every one of these cop shows that I did always ended with a chase, usually a car chase or a foot chase, usually a car chase that would go, you know, two or sometimes three minutes. So you know oh God I’ve got to do the chase today. So you’d walk into your music studio, okay what is it to look at it or just try to remember — we couldn’t really look at the video, we had already seen it once at the studio. All we had was a cue sheet of all the significant dialogue in a specific scene. So I’d go down and recall virtually, and everything’s indicated. All significant action and dialogue is enumerated in this cue sheet. And then you know okay this happens there and then you do all this math. I mean that took half a day sometimes to just block out a big chase cue. Then, now you’ve got to go back to bar one and start writing the actual music.
